data.description: We present the first comprehensive geolocated multi-modal transport database for the whole continent of Africa, the African Transport Systems Database (AfTS-Db), including road, rail, aviation, maritime and inland waterway networks. To do so, we created and standardized asset and network data across all transport modes, including inter-modal connections, attributes of road and rail corridors and estimated annual statistics for airports and ports. The African Transport Systems Database includes 234 airports including their airline routes, 179 maritime ports and their connections with each other, 132 inland ports and docking sites with river and lake connections, 4,412 railway stations connected across 99,373 kilometers of rail lines, and 1,004,512 kilometers of roads mainly comprised of all motorways, trunk roads, primary and secondary routes across Africa and some local roads that connect to other transport modes. The AfTS-Db provides key information for transport planning, resilience assessments, asset management and development of transport models and applications. Furthermore, we expect the data will also be of relevance for environmental, health, social and economic studies.

    <meta name="dc.description" content="We present the first comprehensive geolocated multi-modal transport database for the whole continent of Africa, the African Transport Systems Database (AfTS-Db), including road, rail, aviation, maritime and inland waterway networks.         <div class="c-article-body">
            <section aria-labelledby="Abs1" data-title="Abstract" lang="en"><div class="c-article-section" id="Abs1-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Abs1">Abstract</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Abs1-content"><p>We present the first comprehensive geolocated multi-modal transport database for the whole continent of Africa, the African Transport Systems Database (AfTS-Db), including road, rail, aviation, maritime and inland waterway networks. To do so, we created and standardized asset and network data across all transport modes, including inter-modal connections, attributes of road and rail corridors and estimated annual statistics for airports and ports. The African Transport Systems Database includes 234 airports including their airline routes, 179 maritime ports and their connections with each other, 132 inland ports and docking sites with river and lake connections, 4,412 railway stations connected across 99,373 kilometers of rail lines, and 1,004,512 kilometers of roads mainly comprised of all motorways, trunk roads, primary and secondary routes across Africa and some local roads that connect to other transport modes. The AfTS-Db provides key information for transport planning, resilience assessments, asset management and development of transport models and applications. Furthermore, we expect the data will also be of relevance for environmental, health, social and economic studies.</p></div></div></section>

                        <section data-title="Background"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec1-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec1">Background</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec1-content"><p>Transport networks are lifeline systems that enable mobility of people and facilitate the movement of goods, thereby enabling development benefits and economic growth<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1" title="Hallegatte, S., Rentschler, J. & Rozenberg, J. Lifelines: The resilient infrastructure opportunity, 
                  https://doi.org/10.1596/978-1-4648-1430-3
                  
                 (World Bank, 2019)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR1" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e455">1</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2" title="Van Laak, D. Lifelines of our society: A global history of infrastructure, 
                  https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/14693.001.0001
                  
                 (MIT Press, 2023)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR2" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e458">2</a></sup>. The expansion and modernization of these transport networks form part of most countries’ economic development strategies, especially for countries in Africa<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 3" title="Quium, A. A. Transport corridors for wider socio–economic development. Sustainability 11(19), 5248, 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/su11195248
                  
                 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR3" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e462">3</a></sup>. Transport infrastructure investment, by public bodies and private investors, in Africa has been steadily increasing in monetary value over the past decades<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 4" title="Ijjasz-Vasquez, E. J. Saghir, J. & Noble, I. State and Trends in Adaptation Report 2021: Africa. Global Center for Adaptation 
                  https://gca.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/GCA_STA_2021_Complete_website.pdf
                  
                 (2021)" href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR4" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e466">4</a></sup>. For example, investments in port projects across Africa with private participation grew between 2012–2022 to US$ 12.7 billion from US$ 7.3 billion between 2002–2012<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 5" title="Africa Finance Corporation. The state of Africa’s infrastructure report 2024 (Africa Finance Corporation, 2024)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e470">5</a></sup>. This aligns with the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) project agenda for 2063 to create a single market of 1.3 billion people and a combined GDP of US$ 3.4 trillion across 55 African countries. Investments in transport infrastructure are critical to achieve this, particularly to support industrialization, job creation, and enhanced competitiveness<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 6" title="International Trade Centre (ITC). Made by Africa: Creating Value through Integration. ITC, Geneva. ISBN: 978-92-1-103688-6 (2022)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR6" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e474">6</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 7" title="African Union. African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). African Union 
                  https://au-afcfta.org/
                  
                 (accessed February 2025)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR7" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e477">7</a></sup>. Recognizing this need, the African Development Bank (AfDB) has invested over US$ 13 billion between 2004 and 2022 in regional strategic road corridor projects to improve connectivity, strengthen market accessibility across countries and integrate supply chains<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 8" title="AfDB. Expanding Market Access in Africa and Nurturing Continental Integration. African Development Bank (2023)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR8" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e482">8</a></sup>. This is complemented by other investment initiatives such as, amongst others, the World Bank (approximately US$ 2 billion approved investments in transport projects between 2006 and 2024)<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="World Bank. Zambia - Transport Corridors for Economic Resilience Project (English). Washington, D.C.: World Bank Group 
                  http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/099013124091024437
                  
                 (2024)." href="#ref-CR9" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e486">9</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="World Bank.                   http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/420311468008746849

Kenya - Eastern Africa Regional Transport, Trade and Development Facilitation Program Project: environmental and social impact assessments for three sections: Lesseru-Marich Pass; Marich Pass-Lodwar; and Lodwar-Nakodok - executive summary (English). Washington, DC; World Bank Group 
                  http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/865181468194649905
                  
                 (2015)." href="#ref-CR11" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e486_2">11</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="World Bank. World Bank approves US$90 million additional financing for Djibouti Regional Economic Corridor. 
                  https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2024/09/19/world-bank-approves-us-90-million-additional-financing-for-djibouti-regional-economic-corridor

Tunisia - Road Transport Corridors Project (English). Washington, D.C.: World Bank Group 
                  http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/294541468187792993

                 (accessed February 2025)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR15" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e493">15</a></sup>, China’s Belt and Road initiative (which has invested US$ 53 billion in transport projects across Africa between 2000–2023)<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 16" title="Cabestan, J. P. The Belt and Road Initiative and China’s Hegemony in Africa. Orbis 67(4), 544–564, 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.orbis.2023.08.005
                  
                 (2023)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR16" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e497">16</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 17" title="Boston University Global Development Policy Center. Chinese Loans to Africa Database. 
                  http://bu.edu/gdp/chinese-loans-to-africa-database
                  
                 (2023)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR17" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e500">17</a></sup> and United States’ (US) investments in the Lobito corridor in Southern Africa (US$ 1 billion)<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 18" title="Nsakaza, K. & Maponga, O. The Lobito Corridor as an Anchor of Economic and Value Chain Development in Angola, Democratic Republic of Congo, and Zambia: Exploring the Issues. South African Journal of Economics, 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/saje.12402
                  
                 (2025)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR18" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e504">18</a></sup>.</p><p>Though the initiatives mentioned above are bringing new investments in Africa’s transport sector, the existing investment is well below Africa’s transport needs which have been unable to keep up with the continent’s increasing population, urbanization and trade<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 19" title="Africa Finance Corporation (AFC). State of Africa’s Infrastructure Report 2024. 
                  https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/afc-assets/afc/AFC-State-of-Africas-Infrastructure-2024.pdf
                  
                 (Africa Finance Corporation, 2024)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR19" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e511">19</a></sup>. Estimates suggest that the transport investment needs in Africa in 2020 were between US$ 37–49 billion compared to the actual commitment of US$ 33 billion, resulting in an investment gap of US$ 4–16 billion<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 20" title="African Development Bank Group. Infrastructure Financing Trends in Africa 2019–2020. African Development Bank Group. 
                  https://www.afdb.org/en/documents/infrastructure-financing-trends-africa-2019-2020
                  
                 (2022)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR20" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e515">20</a></sup>. Transport investments in Africa have mostly concentrated around maritime ports to enhance existing or new hubs, while the integration with the road and rail linkages has been underfunded and underdeveloped<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 19" title="Africa Finance Corporation (AFC). State of Africa’s Infrastructure Report 2024. 
                  https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/afc-assets/afc/AFC-State-of-Africas-Infrastructure-2024.pdf
                  
                 (Africa Finance Corporation, 2024)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR19" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e519">19</a></sup>.</p><p>While improvement and development of transport networks can lead to economic growth, regional integration and market expansion, the design and planning of such infrastructure needs to be integrated with considerations of their resilience to climate change, biodiversity and environmental impacts, CO<sub>2</sub> emissions, social exclusion and displacement<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 21" title="Laurance, W. F., Sloan, S., Weng, L. & Sayer, J. A. Estimating the environmental costs of Africa’s massive development corridors. Current Biology 25.24, 3202–3208 (2015)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR21" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e528">21</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 22" title="Churchill, S. A., Inekwe, J., Ivanovski, K. & Smyth, R. Transport infrastructure and CO2 emissions in the OECD over the long run. Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment 95, 102857 (2021)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR22" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e531">22</a></sup>. Transport infrastructures development and quality improvements have been shown to have positive impacts on intra-Africa trade and movements of people<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 23" title="Takpara, M. M., Nkemgha, G. Z., Zouri, S. & Kebalo, L. Transport infrastructure and intra-African trade: A new empirical evidence (Afreximbank Policy Research Working Paper Series No. APRWPS/2024/11). African Export-Import Bank (2024)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR23" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e535">23</a></sup>. To some extent wider social benefits of integrated transport corridor development in Africa is also seen, enabling access to schools, health facilities, communities, supporting local businesses and households, and consequently supporting the general social welfare<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 24" title="African Development Bank. Developing economic corridors in Africa: Rationale for the participation of the AfDB (Regional Integration Brief) 
                  https://www.afdb.org/fileadmin/uploads/afdb/Documents/Publications/Regional_Integration_Brief_-_Developing_Economic_Corridors_in_Africa_-_Rationale_for_the_Participation_of_the_AfDB.pdf
                  
                 (2013)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e539">24</a></sup>. However, there is also compelling evidence to suggest that ongoing large-scale transport corridor developments are causing social exclusion where these corridors do not arrive for marginalized groups or do not benefit vulnerable groups<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 25" title="Enns, C. Mobilizing research on Africa’s development corridors. Geoforum 88, 105–108 (2018)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR25" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e543">25</a></sup>. Research also suggests that there is low integration of future climate risks and adaptation planning across transport projects in East Africa<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 26" title="Bignoli, D. J. et al. Towards more sustainable and inclusive development corridors in Africa. Environmental Research: Infrastructure and Sustainability 4(3), 035012, 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoforum.2017.11.017
                  
                 (2024)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR26" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e548">26</a></sup>, which might lock-in patterns of development in undesirable ways leading to maladaptation<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 27" title="Hall, J. W., Nicholls, R. J., Tran, M. & Hickford, A. J. The Future of National Infrastructure: A System-of-Systems Approach. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781107588745
                  
                 (Cambridge Univ. Press, 2016)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR27" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e552">27</a></sup>.</p><p>To make the case for improving transport investments in Africa and to adequately assess, and mitigate, their impacts, there is a need for open-access data that maps the existing and planned transport networks together<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 26" title="Bignoli, D. J. et al. Towards more sustainable and inclusive development corridors in Africa. Environmental Research: Infrastructure and Sustainability 4(3), 035012, 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoforum.2017.11.017
                  
                 (2024)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR26" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e559">26</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 28" title="Thorn, J. P. R., Mwangi, B. & Juffe Bignoli, D. The African Development Corridors Database. Dryad. Dataset 
                  https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.9kd51c5hw
                  
                 (2022)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR28" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e562">28</a></sup>. Such data needs to be geospatial, on an asset level, and establish connectivity between assets, in order to provide a comparison of the patterns of development across Africa. Elsewhere, some global and continent level initiatives have adopted geospatial network approaches, such as the Global Infrastructure Impact Viewer<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 29" title="UNEP-WCMC. Global Infrastructure Impact Viewer (GIIV). 
                  https://www.giiviewer.org/
                  
                 (Cambridge, UK: UNEP-WCMC, 2022; accessed May 2025)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR29" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e566">29</a></sup>, the European Transport Maps<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 30" title="Baltic Press. European Transport Maps. 
                  https://www.europeantransportmaps.com/
                  
                 (accessed May 2025)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR30" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e570">30</a></sup> and TENtec Information System<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 31" title="European Commission. TENtec Interactive Map Viewer. 
                  https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/tentec-maps/web/public/screen/home
                  
                 (accessed May 2025)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR31" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e574">31</a></sup>, the Asian Transport Observatory<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 32" title="Asian Transport Observatory. Asian Transport Observatory. 
                  https://asiantransportobservatory.org/
                  
                 (Asian Development Bank, 2024; accessed May 2025)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR32" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e578">32</a></sup>, to inform the assessment and management of strategic road and rail corridors<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 33" title="Baranzelli, C. et al. Identification, characterisation and ranking of Strategic Corridors in Africa. EUR 31069 EN, Publications Office of the European Union, Luxembourg, ISBN 978-92-76-52430-4, 
                  https://doi.org/10.2760/498757
                  
                 (2022)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR33" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e583">33</a></sup>. Providing integrated spatial network data could help demonstrate how new developments would affect trade and passenger mobility choices in the future and link economic centers and investment areas to regional markets and ports. However, for Africa there is a general lack of Geographical Information Systems (GIS) data that is standardized and supported by a modelling process that utilizes reliable open-access information and could be updated in the future<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Guigoz, Y. et al. Spatial data infrastructures in. Africa: A gap analysis. Journal of environmental informatics 30(1), 53–62 (2017)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e587">34</a></sup>.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Existing databases and platforms for Africa"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec2-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec2">Existing databases and platforms for Africa</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec2-content"><p>Various platforms and research papers provide valuable data on Africa’s transport sector. However, they do not encompass the entire continent or lack information necessary for geospatial mapping of existing assets and new developments. A brief description of these studies and their content and limitations is provided below and listed in Supplementary Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#MOESM1">S1</a>.</p><p>The UNCTADstat database managed by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) provides trade and transport statistics for African countries, including data on multimodal freight movements<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 35" title="UNCTAD. United Nations Conference on Trade and Development. Trade-and-Transport Dataset (experimental). UNCTADstat. 
                  https://unctadstat.unctad.org/EN/Index.html
                  
                 (accessed November 2024)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR35" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e605">35</a></sup>. Mphigalale (2020)<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 36" title="Mphigalale, T. V. Infrastructure investment in Sub-Saharan Africa: Opportunities, risks and prospects for economic development (2020)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR36" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e609">36</a></sup> conducted both qualitative and quantitative analyses to evaluate private and public infrastructure investment needs and challenges in three countries – Angola, Democratic Republic of Congo and Ghana. However, these datasets are not spatial, limiting their use for planning purposes. At the national scale, some literature is found that assesses railway information, in Ghana<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 37" title="Obeng, D. A., Bessah, E., Amponsah, W., Dzisi, E. K. & Agyare, W. A. Ghana’s railway transport services delivery: A review. Transportation Engineering 8, 100111 (2022)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR37" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e613">37</a></sup> and Nigeria<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 38" title="Dina, A. O. & Raji, B. A. Analysis of train speed performance on Nigeria railway corporation Lagos district narrow gauge track. Ethiopian Journal of Environmental Studies and Management, 9(2) (2017)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR38" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e617">38</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 39" title="Ogochukwu, C. G., Ogochukwu, O. F., Ogorchukwu, I. M. & Ebuka, I. A. Assessment of the performance of railway transportation in Nigeria from 1970 to 2010. Scientific African 15, e01120, 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sciaf.2022.e01120
                  
                 (2022)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR39" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e620">39</a></sup>. In Ethiopia, Аmah (2023)<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 40" title="Аmah, A. M. Challenges and Prospects of Multimodal Transport System in Ethiopia. BRICS Transport. 2(2), 1–6 (2023)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR40" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e624">40</a></sup> characterized the existing state of the main types of land transport (road and rail), and analyzed external and internal factors influencing the formation of variants of the multimodal transport network scheme. These studies either consider old versions of network datasets or are limited to national scales only.</p><p>The African Regional Integration Index (ARII) seeks to assess the status of electricity, transportation, information and communication technologies, and water and sanitation at the national and regional level<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 41" title="African Union, AfDB, UNECA. Africa regional integration index report 2019. 
                  https://www.integrate-africa.org/fileadmin/uploads/afdb/Documents/ARII-Report2019-FIN-R40-11jun20.pdf
                  
                 (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR41" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e631">41</a></sup>. The data is currently available only at the national level and lacks a detailed geographical breakdown<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 42" title="African Development Bank. ARII. Integrate Africa. 
                  https://www.integrate-africa.org/
                  
                 (accessed February 2025) (b)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR42" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e635">42</a></sup>. Similarly, the African Infrastructure Development Index (AIDI) tracks progress of infrastructure development across countries, through high-level non-spatial statistics<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 43" title="AfDB. The Africa Infrastructure Development Index (AIDI) (2018)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR43" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e639">43</a></sup>. The African Infrastructure Knowledge Portal<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 44" title="African Development Bank. AIKP. Infrastructure Africa. 
                  https://infrastructureafrica.opendataforafrica.org/
                  
                 (accessed February 2025) (a)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR44" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e643">44</a></sup> provides limited access to rail data and open access to ports and air transport data by facility at the continental level, reporting the capacity (people or tons of material) and transported freight value. The OurAirport<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 45" title="OurAirports. Airport data. 
                  https://ourairports.com/
                  
                 (accessed June 2025)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR45" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e647">45</a></sup> project is an open-source, global airports geodatabase with size specifications (very small, small, medium, large and other smaller airports). It is continuously updated by users, and it is a very complete dataset in terms of number of airports, while it does not contain additional information on internal and international routes or some quantified measure of usage (e.g. flight numbers or passenger seats offered on flights).</p><p>A number of AfDB supported initiatives provide map-based information on the ongoing transport development projects in Africa. MapAfrica maps the various transport projects and associates them with temporal and technical data on the risk category, funders, and beneficiaries of each project<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 46" title="African Development Bank. MapAfrica. 
                  https://mapafrica.afdb.org/en
                  
                 (accessed February 2025) (c)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR46" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e654">46</a></sup>. However, it omits the actual spatial coverage of projects, often giving only a point location of the region where the project is happening. The African Infrastructure Database (AID) spatially tracks transport projects, but it does not provide a sense of how these projects integrate with the rest of transport networks in Africa<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 47" title="AU-PIDA. African Union. PIDA projects. AU-PIDA 
                  https://www.au-pida.org/pida-projects/
                  
                 (accessed February 2025)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR47" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e658">47</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 48" title="AUDA-NEPAD. African Union Development Agency. African Infrastructure Map. African Infrastructure Database 
                  https://aid.nepad.org/welcome/project-mapping/
                  
                 (accessed November 2024)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR48" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e661">48</a></sup>. Important cross-border road corridors in the African continent are identified by two African Development Bank reports, complete with characteristics such as length and costs of the projects, together with maps illustrating their development in space. This information is useful for understanding continental integration of road corridors, though it is not available as a GIS data resource<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 8" title="AfDB. Expanding Market Access in Africa and Nurturing Continental Integration. African Development Bank (2023)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR8" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e665">8</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 49" title="AfDB. Cross-border Road Corridors: The Quest to Integrate Africa (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR49" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e668">49</a></sup>. Thorn <i>et al</i>.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 28" title="Thorn, J. P. R., Mwangi, B. & Juffe Bignoli, D. The African Development Corridors Database. Dryad. Dataset 
                  https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.9kd51c5hw
                  
                 (2022)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR28" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e675">28</a></sup> (<a href="https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.9kd51c5hw">https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.9kd51c5hw</a>)<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 28" title="Thorn, J. P. R., Mwangi, B. & Juffe Bignoli, D. The African Development Corridors Database. Dryad. Dataset 
                  https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.9kd51c5hw
                  
                 (2022)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR28" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e687">28</a></sup> first mapped development corridors in Africa, creating a comprehensive open-source geo-database of 184 projects, including railways, ports, pipelines, airports, techno-cities, and industrial parks. The database, with 22 attributes, synthesizes data from multiple sources and has also served as a valuable resource for our work. Similarly, the AidData initiative has provided a useful global open-source spatial dataset mapping and tracking China’s development Aid projects linked with OpenStreetMap information<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 50" title="Goodman, S., Zhang, S., Malik, A. A., Parks, B. C. & Hall, J. AidData’s Geospatial Global Chinese Development Finance Dataset. Scientific Data 11(1), 529, 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-024-03341-w
                  
                 (2024)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR50" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e691">50</a></sup>. However, these studies and datasets also do not integrate the projects with the existing networks in Africa. A database compiled by the United States Geological Survey (USGS), focusing on the mineral industries and related infrastructure in Africa<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 51" title="Padilla, A. D. et al. Compilation of geospatial data (GIS) for the mineral industries and related infrastructure of Africa. US Geological Survey. 
                  https://doi.org/10.5066/P97EQWXP
                  
                 (2021)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR51" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e695">51</a></sup>, includes detailed layers of ports, roads, and railways across the continent. However, the USGS database also does not provide much information on the road and rail network attributes and their connectivity to mines and ports, which are provided in our database.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Aim of the current work"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec3-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec3">Aim of the current work</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec3-content"><p>Given that the available data on transportation infrastructure is both sparse and fragmented, a comprehensive open dataset is urgently needed for planning future projects and conducting high level studies supporting more analysis across the African continent. This lack of comprehensive data presents significant challenges for researchers, policymakers, and developers who are trying to understand the broader transportation landscape. Without detailed information on existing infrastructures - such as their condition, usage statistics, and connectivity - it becomes difficult to make informed decisions about where investments are most needed. Moreover, this fragmented approach undermines the potential for regional collaboration and integration of transport networks, which could greatly enhance efficiency and economic growth. To foster development and improve transportation across Africa, a more unified and detailed dataset is essential. Such data would not only facilitate better planning and resource allocation but also support the creation of social, environmentally and economically sustainable transport solutions that meet the diverse needs of the continent’s growing population.</p><p>To address the above needs, this paper presents a novel database of multimodal transport networks (roads, railways, aviation, inland and maritime waterways) for Africa, combining known open spatial datasets with additional information extracted from reports, including existing and approved and already financed infrastructure projects (see Supplementary Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#MOESM1">S2</a>). These transport networks are conceptualized as the collection and interconnection of physical assets that operate in a coordinated way to provide specific infrastructure services<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 27" title="Hall, J. W., Nicholls, R. J., Tran, M. & Hickford, A. J. The Future of National Infrastructure: A System-of-Systems Approach. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781107588745
                  
                 (Cambridge Univ. Press, 2016)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR27" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e713">27</a></sup>. The networks consist of nodes (representing key point locations of physical facilities such as road junctions, railway stations, ports and airports) and links (representing physical connections between nodes such as road sections, railway lines, airline and waterway routes). The multimodal transport system is then created by identifying nodes based on their functionality and proximity to create a network-of-networks<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 52" title="Pant, R., Hall, J. W. & Blainey, S. P. Vulnerability assessment framework for interdependent critical infrastructures: case-study for Great Britain’s rail network. European Journal of Transportation and Infrastructure Research 16(1), 174–194 (2016)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR52" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e717">52</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 53" title="Thacker, S., Pant, R. & Hall, J. W. System-of-systems formulation and disruption analysis for multi-scale critical national infrastructures. Reliability Engineering & System Safety 167, 30–41 (2017)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR53" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e720">53</a></sup>.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Methods"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec4-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec4">Methods</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec4-content"><p>The Africa Transport Systems Database (AfTS-Db) is a geolocated interconnected transport asset and network database for the African continent. The steps to create the AfTS-Db are as follows:</p><ol class="u-list-style-none">
                <li>
                  <span class="u-custom-list-number">1.</span>
                  
                    <p>Create workflows to gather existing open-access reliable transport GIS data for the entire African continent for different transport modes (roads, railways, waterways and airlines).</p>
                  
                </li>
                <li>
                  <span class="u-custom-list-number">2.</span>
                  
                    <p>Collect attributes of interest, to identify names, physical characteristics and usage information of important assets across transport modes.</p>
                  
                </li>
                <li>
                  <span class="u-custom-list-number">3.</span>
                  
                    <p>Create and assemble spatial information on major road corridors and rail routes, together with airports and ports, from various African countries.</p>
                  
                </li>
                <li>
                  <span class="u-custom-list-number">4.</span>
                  
                    <p>Standardize and integrate all datasets to a common network specification, specifying nodes and edges of each transport mode.</p>
                  
                </li>
                <li>
                  <span class="u-custom-list-number">5.</span>
                  
                    <p>Create multimodal connections across the different transport networks.</p>
                  
                </li>
              </ol></div></div></section><section data-title="Search strategy and data manipulation"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec5-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec5">Search strategy and data manipulation</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec5-content"><p>The development of the AfTS-Db follows a structured approach to ensure accuracy, consistency, and comprehensiveness (see Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#Fig1">1</a>). For roads and railways networks, the process begins with extraction of data from OpenStreetMap (OSM)<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 54" title="Open Street Maps. Open Street Maps. 
                  https://download.geofabrik.de/
                  
                 (2021)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR54" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e800">54</a></sup>, converting it into topological networks and enriching attributes in the OSM data with other relevant reports and datasets where geographic and network-related data are gathered. OSM is an open-source, open-contributors dataset mapping the world, particularly useful for road and rail infrastructures geographical data and widely used for the transport sector analysis<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 55" title="Barron, C., Neis, P. & Zipf, A. A comprehensive framework for intrinsic OpenStreetMap quality analysis. Transactions in GIS 18(6), 877–895 (2014)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR55" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e804">55</a></sup>. New or additional projects from other sources<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 28" title="Thorn, J. P. R., Mwangi, B. & Juffe Bignoli, D. The African Development Corridors Database. Dryad. Dataset 
                  https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.9kd51c5hw
                  
                 (2022)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR28" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e808">28</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 47" title="AU-PIDA. African Union. PIDA projects. AU-PIDA 
                  https://www.au-pida.org/pida-projects/
                  
                 (accessed February 2025)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR47" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e811">47</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 50" title="Goodman, S., Zhang, S., Malik, A. A., Parks, B. C. & Hall, J. AidData’s Geospatial Global Chinese Development Finance Dataset. Scientific Data 11(1), 529, 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-024-03341-w
                  
                 (2024)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR50" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e814">50</a></sup> are added to the OSM networks. Further attributes, such as names of specific road corridors and railway lines, railway station facilities based on the type of usage (e.g. a dry port station or a station at a mine location) are added to OSM network assets (nodes and edges) from different sources<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 8" title="AfDB. Expanding Market Access in Africa and Nurturing Continental Integration. African Development Bank (2023)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR8" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e818">8</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 49" title="AfDB. Cross-border Road Corridors: The Quest to Integrate Africa (2019)." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR49" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e821">49</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 56" title="Young, M. An Open Source Routable Rail Dataset For Africa. 
                  https://github.com/trg-rail/africa_rail_network
                  
                ." href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#ref-CR56" id="ref-link-section-d17845791e824">56</a></sup>. For waterways and airlines networks other known open datasets (see below) are gathered and different attributes from these datasets are combined to create consistent datasets. Each transport mode dataset consists of a node layer (for point assets) and an edge layer (for line connections) with common column names and attributes that are standardized across all modes (see Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/articles/s41597-025-06483-7#Tab2">2</a>).</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-1" data-title="Fig. 1"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig1" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 1</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><picture class="c-article-section__figure-picture"><source type="image/webp" srcset="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41597-025-06483-7/MediaObjects/41597_2025_6483_Fig1_HTML.png?as=webp"><img aria-describedby="figure-1-desc
